catalog_quote: Stress in Yuki is non-contrastive and predictable. ... The domain of primary stress is the root of the Yuki word. Primary stress typically occurs in the initial syllable of the root, though some variation is seen for words containing roots of more than syllable. As Yuki is primarily a suffixing language, the root is usually the first syllable of the word, regardless of word class. Suffixes and enclitics do not alter the position of stress, thus primary stress is typically found in the initial syllable of a word. ... In prefixed words, the body prefixes are unstressed with primary stress remaining on the root. ... The possessive prefix is unstressed with primary stress falling on the initial syllable of the noun root. ... Schlichter (1978:16) describes primary stress in reduplicated forms as occurring on the second syllable, while the reduplicant is the unstressed initial syllable. Lexic…

tone_statements.quote: Yuki phonemes … Based on data collected Dec. 1955 by S. Lamb … vowel length: · Tones: high ´ low ` rising ˇ falling ˆ … Tones we must at least set up /´/ and /ˆ/ : ṭ'ól hair α23 : hûl eyes α23 . there is probably no /ˇ/ (not in Yuki either), as rises seem to always start fairly high anyway, and are probably variants of /´/. It is perhaps not necessary to set up /`/. unmarked vowels would be said to have low pitch. this would be the neutral condition.

tone_statements.quote: In an unpublished note in 1933, Uldall suggested that Yuki was a tone language, but Schlichter has concluded that the tone is an effect of stress. tone_statements.citation: Schlichter, Alice. 1978. Is Yuki a tone language? Unpublished manuscript (cited by Balodis 2016:58-59, 63, 656).
tone_statements.quote: 6, I have argued that Yuki is neither a tone nor a pitch- … accent language, It is a stress-accent language whose main perceptual cue of cumulative stress is very high pitch for primary accent, mid to high pitch for se- … condary accent, There is one primary accent per word, and the placement of both primary. and secondary accent is predictable in terms of grammatical and phonetic factors and has no lexical function, When Yuki, became moribund, it was in the process of tonogenesis, developing a phonemic … contrast between high-level and high-falling tone,
tone_statements.locator: ms pp. 24-25, sec. 6 Conclusions; supporting: sec. 4 ms p. 21; sec. 2 ms pp. 6-7 'Thus Yuki is not a language with phonemic tone, is not a tone language'.
tone_statements.summary: Not a tone or pitch accent language: one predictable primary accent per word, cued mainly by very high pitch; fast-speech V?V contraction gives incipient high-level vs high-falling pairs, not lexical.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Balodis 2016 text we hold at the cited sections/pages (§1.7 p.37; §2.2.1.1 pp.57-59 incl. fn.63; §2.2.1.2 p.62; fn.74 p.63), including the source's own typo 'roots of more than syllable'. (2) The classification (morphological: root-initial primary stress, prefixes/possessive prefixes/reduplicants unstressed, suffixes and enclitics inert, listed exceptions for disyllabic roots and lexicalized compounds) rests on a 2016 UC Press reference grammar that includes the author's own acoustic measurements; for a dormant language with no other grammar or phonology in Glottolog 5.1, this is the best source that can exist, and we hold it. (3) The only unheld items are the older primary materials Balodis himself digests (Sawyer & Schlichter 1984:11, Schlichter 1985 diss., Schlichter 1978 ms); none is likely to change the classification, so they are low-priority. tone.quote: Recent analysis of the Yuki language materials recorded in 1931-32 from Ralph Moore in collaboration with the late Hans Uldall reveal three structural traits more or less reminiscent of Athabascan. These traits are: tonality; a strong tendency toward monosyllabic morphemes; multiple forms taken by verb stems. The historic Athabascan languages of California are not tonal, but they may once have been; in California these languages had entered an area of prevailingly toneless speech.
